summary: In traffic-engineered networks it is sometimes desirable to set up an end-to-end path with constraints such as bandwidth across several networks. This best current practice document states the problem of exchanging the traffic engineering information needed for that and describes an architecture, including abstraction of topology, for sharing it between interconnected networks. It is a problem statement and architecture, not a new protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: When a path has to cross two or more networks, the network that computes it needs to know what the other networks can offer. RFC 7926 describes a way for each network to publish a filtered, abstract view of its own capacity, and for a middle layer to carry those views so that a path can be computed across the whole set.

subtitle: How networks share just enough traffic engineering information to build a path that crosses them.

tldr.problem: A traffic-engineered path often has to cross several networks, but each network only knows its own topology, so the router that computes the path cannot tell which exit point will actually lead to the destination.
tldr.mechanism: Each network applies policy to its own traffic engineering information and advertises the result as abstract links and abstract nodes. An abstraction layer network sits between the networks, carrying those advertisements so a path can be computed across them.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7926 is BCP 206 and is not obsoleted. It is a problem statement and an architecture, not a protocol, and it deliberately covers only the simple constraints needed to decide reachability.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: TE reachability and simple TE constraints

today: RFC 7926 is a Best Current Practice document, BCP 206, and is neither obsoleted nor updated by any RFC listed for it. It is a problem statement and an architecture rather than a protocol; the protocols it points at include RFC 7752 for BGP-LS and RFC 6107 for signalling the purpose of a path.

sections.title: The Problem: Paths Across Networks
sections.content:
Traffic-Engineered systems such as MPLS-TE and GMPLS offer a way to establish paths through a network in a controlled way that reserves network resources on specified links. TE paths are computed by examining the Traffic Engineering Database and selecting a sequence of links and nodes capable of meeting the requirements of the path. The database is built from information distributed by the Interior Gateway Protocol running in the network, for example OSPF-TE or IS-IS-TE.

It is sometimes desirable to establish an end-to-end TE path that crosses more than one network or administrative domain. In these cases the availability of TE information is usually limited to within each network, and such networks are referred to as domains: a collection of network elements within a common sphere of address management or path computational responsibility, examples of which are IGP areas and Autonomous Systems.

To determine the potential to establish a TE path through a series of connected domains, and to choose the appropriate domain connection points through which to route a path, it is necessary to have a certain amount of TE information about each domain. This need not be the full set of TE information available within each domain, but it does need to express the potential of providing TE connectivity. This subset of TE information is called TE reachability information, and it can be exchanged between domains based on information gathered from the local routing protocol, filtered by configured policy, or statically configured.

The document sets out the problem statement for this exchange and describes the best current practice architecture to meet it. The scope is limited to the simple TE constraints and information, such as TE metrics, hop count, bandwidth, delay and shared risk, necessary to determine TE reachability: discussion of multiple additional constraints that might qualify the reachability can significantly complicate aggregation of information and the stability of the mechanism used to present potential connectivity.
sections.plainLanguage: Each network knows its own links and spare capacity, but not its neighbour's. The document describes what has to be shared for a path to be built across several of them, and deliberately keeps the list short so that the sharing mechanism stays stable.

sections.title: The Terms Used Here
sections.content:
A TE connection is a Label Switched Path through an MPLS-TE or GMPLS network that directs traffic along a particular path, the TE path, in order to provide a specific service such as a bandwidth guarantee, separation of traffic, or resilience between a well-known pair of end points.

TE metrics and TE attributes are terms applied to parameters of links, and possibly nodes, in a network traversed by TE connections, used by path computation algorithms to select the paths that TE connections follow. A TE metric is a quantifiable value describing some property of a link or node that can be used as part of TE routing or planning; a TE attribute is the wider term, covering any property or characteristic of a link or node usable as part of TE routing or planning. The delay introduced by transmission on a link is an example of a TE metric, while the geographic location of a router is an example of a more general attribute. The same terms also describe the end-to-end characteristics of a TE connection, derived from the metrics of the links it traverses: the end-to-end delay is usually the sum of the delay on each link.

TE reachability is the ability to reach a specific address along a TE path, that is, the ability to establish a TE connection. It may be unqualified, meaning there is a TE path but no information about available resources or other constraints, which is helpful in determining a path to a destination that lies in an unknown domain or that may be qualified by attributes and metrics such as hop count, available bandwidth, delay and shared risk.

Aggregation means representing multiple network resources from a domain outside the domain as a single entity. Abstraction is the process of applying policy to the available TE information within a domain to produce selective information representing the potential ability to connect across the domain. An abstract link is the representation of the characteristics of a path between two nodes in a domain produced by abstraction, advertised outside that domain as a TE link for use in signalling in other domains. An abstract node, also called a virtual node, is the representation as a single node in a TE topology of some or all of the resources of one or more nodes and the links that connect them.

The abstraction layer network may be seen as a brokerage-layer network between one or more server networks and one or more client networks. It is the collection of abstract links that provide potential connectivity across the server networks and on which path computation can be performed to determine edge-to-edge paths that provide connectivity as links in the client network.
sections.plainLanguage: The vocabulary distinguishes two ideas that look alike. Aggregation means combining resources into one number, which loses detail. Abstraction means publishing a deliberately selective view that says what the domain is willing to offer. The links published are called abstract links, and the layer that carries them is the abstraction layer.

sections.title: Two Kinds of Relationship: Peers and Client-Server
sections.content:
The peer network use case can be illustrated by a simple example. A TE path is required between a source and a destination located in different domains, with two points of interconnection between the domains, and selecting the wrong point of interconnection can lead to a suboptimal path or even to no path being available. Peer networks are assumed to have the same technology type, that is, the same switching capability.

When Domain A attempts to select a path it may determine that adequate bandwidth is available from the source through both interconnection points, and it may pick the one through x1 for local policy reasons, perhaps because the TE metric is smaller. But if there is no connectivity in Domain Z from x1 to the destination, the path cannot be established. Techniques such as crankback may be used to alleviate this, but they do not lead to rapid setup or guaranteed optimality, and RSVP signalling creates state that is immediately removed by the crankback procedure, so frequent events of this kind impact scalability in a non-deterministic manner.

More complicated examples exist, such as a mesh of domains, where the source domain must be sensitive to the TE connectivity available through each intermediate domain as well as the connectivity from each interconnection point to the destination within the destination domain. The problem is further complicated when the source domain does not know in which domain the destination node is located, since the choice of a domain path depends on knowledge of the destination domain.

Two major classes of use case relate to the client-server relationship between networks, and have sometimes been referred to as overlay networks. In both classes the client and server networks may have the same switching capability, or they may be built from nodes and links with different technology types. In the first group, domains belonging to one network are connected by a domain belonging to another network, and once connectivity is formed across the lower-layer network the domains of the upper-layer network can be merged into a single domain by running IGP adjacencies and treating the server-network-layer connectivity as links in the higher-layer network. The TE relationship between the two layers is then reduced to determining what server network connectivity to establish, how to trigger it, how to route it in the server network, and what resources and capacity to assign within the server network layer.

In the second group, the client network asks the server network for connectivity, using a service request that may carry no metrics, one or more metrics to optimize, absolute constraints, fate diversity or fate sharing requests, concurrent provisioning, or a request for service resilience.
sections.plainLanguage: Two relationships are described. In a peer relationship the networks are equals and each has to guess which of its exit points the next network can actually reach. In a client-server relationship one network is the underlay and the other asks it for a connection, so the underlay can promise something specific.

sections.title: What a Solution Has to Handle
sections.content:
The problem can be stated simply: a mechanism is required that allows TE path computation in one domain to make informed choices about the TE capabilities and exit points from the domain when signalling an end-to-end TE path that will extend across multiple domains. The problem is one of information collection and presentation, not about signalling: the existing signalling mechanisms for TE LSP establishment are likely to prove adequate, and TE information may already be distributed within a domain by TE extensions to one of the two IGPs and exported from a domain using link-state extensions to BGP.

Policy and filters. A solution must be amenable to the application of policy and filters. The operator of a domain sharing information must be able to apply controls to what information is shared, and the operator of a domain that has information shared with it must be able to apply policies and filters to the received information. The path computation within a domain must also be able to weight the information received from other domains according to local policy.

Confidentiality. An operator may desire to keep confidential the details about its internal network topology and loading, which could be construed as commercially sensitive. Although TE information exchange may take place only between parties that have significant trust, there are use cases such as the VPN supported over multiple server network domains where information will be shared between domains that have a commercial relationship but a low level of trust. It must therefore be possible for a domain to limit the shared information to only what the computing domain needs to know, with the understanding that the less information made available the more likely the result is a less optimal path and more crankback events.

Information overload. Networks are partitioned into separate domains to reduce the set of information any one router has to handle, and this applies to the volume of information routing protocols have to distribute. If the solution were to share all TE information between all domains, the effect would be to create one single flat network domain. The solution must therefore deliver enough information to make the computation practical but not so much as to overload the receiving domain, and it cannot simply rely on policies and filters, because such filters might not always be enabled.

Information churn. As LSPs are set up and torn down, the available TE resources on links change, and the computation point must have an up-to-date view of them, but collecting this information may load the distribution protocol and churn the stored information. In packet networks, where the capacity of an LSP is often a small fraction of the resources available on a link, advertising routers can apply a threshold so that they do not update the advertisement unless the change exceeds a configured percentage of the total or remaining resources. In non-packet networks, where link resources are physical switching resources such as timeslots or wavelengths, the capacity of an LSP may more frequently be a significant percentage of the available link resources, and end-to-end resource continuity may be needed, so it is far more desirable to keep the TE information at the computation points up to date. Fortunately, non-packet networks tend to be smaller, with lower arrival rates and longer hold times, so the churn may be sustainable.

Aggregation. Two aggregation mechanisms are often considered. The virtual node model aggregates the domain as if it were a single router, with its links to other domains presented as real TE links, but the model assumes that any LSP entering the virtual node through one link can be routed to leave through any other. The virtual link model reduces the domain to a set of edge-to-edge TE links. Part of the nature of aggregation is that information is removed, which can cause inaccuracies and failed path computation: in the virtual node model there might not actually be a TE path available between a pair of domain entry points, and in the virtual link model it may prove very hard to aggregate multiple link characteristics, since one path may have high bandwidth and another low delay, which does not mean the connectivity should be advertised as having both. The trick is to aggregate in a way that retains as much useful information as possible while removing the data that is not needed, and an important part of that trick is a clear understanding of what information is actually needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Five things can go wrong, and the architecture has to answer each of them. What is shared has to be filterable, and some of it may be commercially secret. What is shared must not be so much that it merges all the domains into one. The information must not change so often that the network cannot keep up. And anything left out of the summary may make a path computation fail.

sections.title: Abstraction Instead of Aggregation
sections.content:
Aggregation is the process of synthesising from available information, so the virtual node and virtual link models rely on processing the information available within a network to produce the aggregate representations presented to the consumer. As described in Section 3, dynamic aggregation is subject to a number of pitfalls. In order to distinguish the architecture described here from the previous work on aggregation, the document uses the term abstraction. The process of abstraction is one of applying policy to the available TE information within a domain, to produce selective information that represents the potential ability to connect across the domain.

Abstraction does not offer all possible connectivity options but does present a general view of potential connectivity. It may have a dynamic element but is not intended to keep pace with the changes in TE attribute availability within the network, so when relying on an abstraction to compute an end-to-end path, the process might not deliver a usable path: there is no actual guarantee that the abstractions are current or feasible.

Although abstraction uses available TE information, it is subject to policy and management choices, so not all potential connectivity will be advertised to each client network. The filters may depend on commercial relationships, the risk of disclosing confidential information, and concerns about what use is made of the connectivity that is offered.
sections.plainLanguage: The architecture deliberately does not summarise the network automatically. It publishes what the operator chooses to publish, on the understanding that a path computed from that view may turn out not to work, and that the operator will notice and adjust.

sections.title: The Abstraction Layer Network
sections.content:
An abstract link is a measure of the potential to connect a pair of points with certain TE parameters; it is a path and its characteristics in the server network, and it represents the possibility of setting up an LSP over which LSPs may then be set up. Since client network nodes have no visibility into the server network, they must rely on the abstraction information delivered to them by the server network, which will report on the potential for connectivity.

The abstraction layer is an intermediary network layer that separates the client network resources from the server network resources. It contains the client network edge nodes, the server network edge nodes, the client-server links, and the abstract links. In the simplest example the diameter of the abstraction layer network is only three hops, but an instance of an IGP could easily be run so that all nodes participating in the abstraction layer, and in particular the client network edge nodes, can see the TE connectivity in the layer.

The client network is able to operate as normal: connectivity across the network can be either found or not found, based on the links that appear in the client network's own database, and if connectivity cannot be found, end-to-end LSPs cannot be set up, which may be reported, but no dynamic action is taken by the client network. The server network also operates as normal: LSPs across it between client network edges are set up in response to management commands or in response to signalling requests. The abstract links are created by the server network according to local policy and represent the potential connectivity that the server network is willing to make available for use by the client network.

When the client network needs additional connectivity, it can make a request to the abstraction layer network. For example, the operator of the client network may want to create a link from one client edge node to another. The abstraction layer can see the potential path and can set up an LSP across the server network and make that LSP available as a link in the client network.

Addressing needs care, because the network layers in this architecture should be able to operate with separate address spaces, and these may overlap without any technical issues: complete address separation between networks. Mapping between address spaces is needed at the interfaces, and requires configuration, so that when the server network announces an abstract link from A to B the abstraction layer network must recognise that A and B are server network addresses and map them to abstraction layer addresses before including the link in its own topology.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a middle layer with its own view of the topology. It holds the abstract links published by the network underneath and the links published to the network above. When the upper network wants a connection, the middle layer asks the lower network to set one up and then advertises it as a link the upper network can use.

sections.title: Building on Existing Protocols
sections.content:
This section is non-normative and is not intended to prejudge a solutions framework or any applicability work. The general principle of protocol reuse is preferred over the invention of new protocols or additional protocol extensions, and it would be advantageous to use an existing protocol that is commonly implemented on network nodes and is currently deployed, or to use existing computational elements such as path computation elements. This has benefits in network stability, time to deployment and operator training. Existing protocols are unlikely to be immediately suitable to this problem space without some extensions, and extending protocols must be done with care and with consideration for the stability of existing deployments; in extreme cases a new protocol can be preferable to a messy hack of an existing protocol.

BGP-LS is a set of extensions to BGP whose purpose is to announce topology information from one network to a northbound consumer. Its application has focused on building a traffic engineering database for a path computation element, but BGP's mechanisms would also serve well to advertise abstract links from a server network into the abstraction layer network, or to advertise potential connectivity from the abstraction layer network to the client network.

Both OSPF and IS-IS have been extended to advertise TE information, and both are capable of running in a multi-instance mode, either as completely separate instances using different address spaces or as dual instances on the same address space. Either could probably be used as the routing protocol in the abstraction layer network. RSVP-TE signalling can be used to set up all TE LSPs demanded by the model without any protocol extensions; if necessary, LSP hierarchy or LSP stitching can be used to carry LSPs over the server network, again without extensions. The procedures of RFC 6107 allow the dynamic signalling of the purpose of any LSP that is established, so that when an LSP tunnel is set up the two ends can coordinate into which routing protocol instance it should be advertised and can agree on the addressing to be used to identify the link that will be created.
sections.plainLanguage: The document does not invent anything. The pieces already exist: BGP extensions can carry the published topology northbound, the two interior gateway protocols can run inside the abstraction layer, and the existing reservation protocol can set up the connections. Only small extensions may be needed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security of signalling and routing protocols is usually administered and achieved within the boundaries of a domain. A domain with a GMPLS control plane would apply the security mechanisms and considerations appropriate to GMPLS. Domain-based security relies strongly on ensuring that control-plane messages are not allowed to enter the domain from outside.

The additional considerations arising from this document relate to the exchange of control-plane information between domains. Messages are passed between domains using control-plane protocols operating between peers that have predictable relationships, for example between a client-facing interface and a network-facing interface, between BGP-LS speakers, or between peer domains. The security that needs additional attention for inter-domain TE therefore concentrates on authentication of peers, assertion that messages have not been tampered with, and, to a lesser extent, protecting the content of the messages from inspection, since that might give away sensitive information about the networks. The protocols likely to provide the foundation for solutions to this architecture already include such protection and can also be run over protected transports such as IPsec, Transport Layer Security and the TCP Authentication Option.

The control plane of the abstraction layer network is likely to be out of band, that is, control-plane messages will be exchanged over network links that are not the links to which they apply, and the security mechanisms can be applied to the protocols operating in that out-of-band network.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside a domain, security is the domain's own business. Between domains, three things matter: proving who is on the other end, proving the messages were not altered, and keeping the contents private where they reveal sensitive detail. The control traffic of the middle layer will usually run on links other than the ones it describes, which helps.

viz.caption: THE FIVE ISSUES A SOLUTION MUST HANDLE

items.title: Policy and filters
items.text: The operator must control what is shared, and be able to filter what arrives.

items.title: Confidentiality
items.text: Topology and loading may be commercially sensitive, so a domain can share only what is needed.

items.title: Information overload
items.text: Sharing everything would merge the domains into one flat network.

items.title: Information churn
items.text: Capacity changes constantly; thresholds and update intervals keep the load down.

items.title: Aggregation
items.text: Summarising loses detail, so the summary may be wrong in ways that break a path.

viz.caption: THE EXISTING PROTOCOLS THE ARCHITECTURE CAN REUSE

items.title: BGP-LS
items.text: Announces topology to a northbound consumer, and would serve well to advertise abstract links.

items.title: OSPF-TE and IS-IS-TE
items.text: Both carry TE information and can run as separate instances, so either could route the abstraction layer.

items.title: RSVP-TE
items.text: Can set up all the TE paths the model demands without any protocol extension.

items.title: LSP hierarchy and stitching
items.text: Carry paths over the server network, again without extensions.

items.title: Signalling of LSP purpose
items.text: Lets the two ends agree on how the new link is advertised and addressed.
